When the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, the side facing us is mostly or completely dark — that's a new moon, and it's not visible except during daylight. As the Moon moves around Earth, more of its sunlit side comes into view — first a thin sliver (the first quarter), then half (the full moon), then the second half (the last quarter), and finally back to a slim sliver on the other side. This cycle takes about 29.5 days, which is why we have about two moons per month that appear to change shape. The apparent size of the Moon doesn't change much — that consistent disk is what gives the full moon its name.
